blocks.text: When farmers in the middle belt burn a field at the end of the dry season, carbon that sat in grass stems for months shoots into the air as carbon dioxide in a few minutes. When an oil pipeline ruptures in the Niger Delta, that same carbon, locked as crude oil for millions of years, smothers mangroves and fish ponds. Nutrient cycles keep elements moving; pollution and wasteful use jam the cycles — and conservation is how we keep them working.

blocks.markdown:
## The carbon cycle

Carbon moves between the air, living things, soil and fossil fuels.

**Photosynthesis** pulls carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and builds it into carbohydrate in green plants. Animals obtain that carbon by eating plants or other animals. **Respiration** in plants, animals and microbes returns carbon dioxide to the air. **Decomposition** of dead organisms by bacteria and fungi also releases carbon dioxide (and methane in waterlogged soil). **Combustion** of wood, charcoal, petrol and gas — including bush burning and generator exhaust — oxidises carbon compounds rapidly to carbon dioxide.

Over geological time, some carbon is locked as coal, oil and limestone. Burning fossil fuels and cutting rainforest faster than it regrows raise atmospheric carbon dioxide and contribute to global warming.

blocks.title: Nitrogen fixation
blocks.text: The conversion of unreactive atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂) into compounds plants can use, chiefly ammonium and nitrate. It is carried out by Rhizobium in the root nodules of legumes such as cowpea and groundnut, by free-living soil bacteria such as Azotobacter, and by lightning, which forms nitrogen oxides that wash into the soil as dilute nitric acid.

rows: Nitrate (and some ammonium) taken up to make protein
Pseudomonas and other denitrifying bacteria in waterlogged soil
Nitrate → N₂ gas, lost to the air
Nitrate washed out of the soil into rivers

blocks.markdown:
## Pollution

**Air pollution.** Carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion in old generators and traffic binds haemoglobin more tightly than oxygen and can kill. Sulphur dioxide from burning fossil fuels dissolves to form acid rain, which damages leaves, corrodes buildings and acidifies ponds. Excess carbon dioxide traps heat.

**Water pollution.** Crude-oil spills in the Niger Delta coat mangrove roots, block gills and poison fish ponds. Untreated sewage and fertiliser runoff add nitrates and phosphates; algae bloom, then die and are decomposed, stripping oxygen from the water — **eutrophication**. Plastic bags clog drains in Lagos and Ibadan and are swallowed by livestock and turtles.

**Soil pollution.** Spent oil, excess agrochemicals and dumped plastic reduce soil fertility and can enter food crops.

items: Afforestation and reforestation replace trees that absorb carbon dioxide and protect soil; they are the opposite of indiscriminate felling.
Laws and agencies (for example NESREA) restrict dumping, logging and trade in endangered species.
National parks and game reserves — Yankari in Bauchi, Cross River National Park, Gashaka-Gumti, Kainji — protect habitats and the species in them.
Recycling paper, metal and plastic reduces the demand for new raw materials and the volume of waste.
Alternative energy (solar, small hydro, biogas) cuts combustion of wood and fossil fuel.
Crop rotation with legumes, contour ploughing and controlled grazing keep soil nitrogen and structure intact.

blocks.title: Tracing nitrogen from air to a plate of moi-moi
blocks.prompt: Cowpea plants used to make moi-moi have root nodules. Trace the pathway by which nitrogen from the air becomes protein in the seed, and state two ways that nitrogen can be lost from that farm soil afterwards.

steps.text: Rhizobium in the cowpea nodules fixes atmospheric N₂ into ammonium compounds the plant can use.
The plant combines that nitrogen with carbohydrate from photosynthesis to synthesise amino acids and then seed protein.

When the pods are harvested, that protein leaves the field on the farmer's plate. Any roots and fallen leaves left behind are decomposed: ammonifying bacteria release ammonia, Nitrosomonas convert it to nitrite and Nitrobacter convert nitrite to nitrate.

Nitrogen is lost from the soil if heavy rain leaches nitrate into streams, if waterlogged conditions allow Pseudomonas to denitrify nitrate back to N₂, or if the whole crop is removed without returning compost or manure.

blocks.answer: Air N₂ → Rhizobium fixation → plant protein in the cowpea seed. Losses: leaching of nitrate, denitrification in waterlogged soil, and removal of the harvested crop.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Do not mix up the nitrogen bacteria: Rhizobium fixes, Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter nitrify (ammonia to nitrite to nitrate), Pseudomonas denitrifies. Combustion returns carbon to the air; photosynthesis removes it. For conservation, name a Nigerian park — Yankari or Cross River — rather than writing 'game reserve' with no example.

points: Carbon cycles through photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition and combustion; burning fossil fuels raises atmospheric CO₂.
Nitrogen gas is fixed by Rhizobium, Azotobacter and lightning; nitrifying bacteria make nitrate; denitrifying bacteria and leaching remove it.
Air pollutants include CO and SO₂; water pollutants include oil spills, sewage and fertiliser that cause eutrophication; plastic pollutes land and water.
Conservation methods include afforestation, laws, national parks such as Yankari and Cross River, recycling and alternative energy.
Legumes in rotation restore soil nitrogen because of their mutualism with Rhizobium.
